An invalid `format`, `audience` or `detail` value (rejected by the registry validator with the accepted enum)
Unavailable indexed evidence
limitations: Unknown facts are explicit, and a required section that renders empty says why in its own words; a document with no cited claim never reports `passed`
Stale evidence is qualified per citation and counted as `freshness.passed: false`; it cannot silently become current
`includeTests` is a real option only where a test section is rendered: `symbol` and `feature`. The other modes refuse it instead of accepting a no-op
`project` mode accepts a target but uses it as document metadata; it does not scope the selection
`feature` mode's semantic candidate expansion is opt-in via `detail: "deep"`; every other call is lexically discovered and says so, because semantic expansion measured 19-52 s on a 310k-symbol index
A scope with more indexed symbols than `2 x limit` reports the selection bound (`selected` of `available`) rather than implying it mapped the whole set
When the required sections cannot fit `maxTokens`, the result is returned with `budget.passed: false` and the smallest honest rendering named; it is never met by dropping a required section
tools.performance: Measured warm on the reference index (6,452 files, 310,423 symbols, 820,040 relationships): default calls take symbol 0.24 s, file 0.19 s, module 0.42 s, api 1.03 s, project 0.76 s, coverage 0.07 s, feature 1.97 s (p50; five runs, p95 at most 3.65 s). A COLD first default call in a fresh process is 3.9 s on a cold page cache (930 ms with a warm one) and the read-only database open is 2 ms; the cold cost is index page-cache warm-up, not query time, and it is declared here rather than hidden by the warm figures. `feature` with `detail: "deep"` adds a semantic candidate pass (measured 18.0 s and 926 MB on the reference index) and is the only shape that can approach the client timeout; the default feature call is lexical and 2 s. Work is bounded by the request: the evidence limit bounds the facts, the per-section cap bounds each section, and `maxTokens` bounds the emitted payload. The default budget is 8,000 tokens because the measured minimum honest rendering of a project document on the reference index is about 6,700 tokens; a 4,000-token default could not be honoured by its own reference call.
tools.safety: Read-only with one bounded, declared exception: when the files a document cites are stale, the handler reindexes exactly those cited files (at most 25 files / 2 MiB per call) and regenerates. `refresh:false` or `BB_NO_AUTO_REFRESH=1` opts out and the answer declares the decline. It never writes source, never creates a file, never calls bb_edit, and never touches a file the document does not cite.
tools.evidence: Claims are classified as extracted, inferred, generated or unknown and carry resolvable citations; relationship facts name the symbol on the other end of the edge, with inbound edges naming the documented symbol. `quality.references` counts the citations the answer emits so the stale/missing numbers can be checked against the Sources list.

tools.name: bb_edit
tools.description: Unified, validated source mutation. Discriminated by mode: write, update, insert, delete, or refactor. Supports dry-run previews, separator/symlink-safe paths, AST byte bounds, caller protection, rollback on validation failure, formatting, and reindexing. If the target file changed since it was indexed, this tool refreshes that one file and re-resolves the symbol before editing (reported in warnings) — an edit is never applied to stale byte bounds, and a symbol that was renamed or removed is refused by name. The bytes each target had when the edit was PLANNED are re-checked immediately before the write, so a file that changed in between (an editor saving during a multi-file refactor, say) is refused with nothing written rather than overwritten from a plan computed against its previous contents. A project with no index is not a dead end: `write` plans from the request and the disk, resolves no symbol, and reindexes the file it wrote (so `reindexed` is how a brand-new project gets its first indexed rows), while `update`, `insert`, `delete` and `refactor` resolve their target through the index and are refused — with the mode that still works named beside the reindex command — until one exists. `write` replacing an existing file is guarded: a replacement that removes at least half of a file's lines (and at least 5 lines) is refused as a probable mistake unless `overwrite: true` is passed, and `overwrite: false` makes the write create-only — the refusal names the file, the line counts and both options. `batch` applies several edits, or one edit across several files, as ONE atomic call: every entry is planned before anything is written (so a refusal anywhere writes nothing), the bytes of EVERY target are re-checked together immediately before the first write, and formatting, validation and reindexing each run ONCE for the whole call. Two entries may not resolve to the same file — each is planned from its file's pre-edit bytes, so the second would discard the first, and that is refused by entry index. Every answer carries a per-file `envelope` (`planned`, `committed`, `restored`, and the pre/post byte counts), and a refused call carries the same envelope on the error, so "is my working tree back?" is answered per file rather than by one boolean. Unlike `write`, `batch` needs an index: the mode cannot promise of a list what a single entry's plan proves.

mode.description: Edit kind: write (create or overwrite a file), update (replace a symbol body), insert (add code relative to a symbol), delete (remove a symbol), refactor (identifier-aware rename), or batch (apply several edits, or one edit across several files, as one atomic call)

dryRun.description: Preview the planned changes without writing any file (default false)

filePath.description: write: project-relative target file to create or overwrite. Other modes: disambiguates symbolName when it appears in multiple files

symbolName.description: Name of the symbol to update, delete, or refactor (the index must contain it; a target file changed since indexing is refreshed automatically before the edit)

lineStart.description: Declaration line of the target symbol, used with symbolName/filePath to disambiguate repeated names

content.description: Full file content for write mode; also accepted in place of newContent for update and insert

newContent.description: Replacement source: update swaps the symbol body for this text; insert adds this text relative to targetSymbolName

targetSymbolName.description: insert: symbol whose body or boundary receives the new code (required for insert)

position.description: insert anchor relative to targetSymbolName (default after)

newName.description: refactor: the valid identifier the symbol is renamed to

force.description: delete: allow removal when indexed callers or live references survive; leftovers are reported as warnings (default false)

format.description: Run the project formatter on written files after the edit (default true)

overwrite.description: write only. Omitted: replace the file, but refuse a replacement that removes at least half of a file's lines and at least 5 lines (a probable mistake, such as a body fragment sent to write instead of update). true: replace it whatever the size. false: create-only — refuse when the file already exists.

edits.description: batch only, required there: the edits to apply, each a complete request in one of the five single-file modes (write|update|insert|delete|refactor), e.g. [{mode:'update',symbolName:'helper',newContent:'...'},{mode:'delete',symbolName:'oldFlag'}]. Entries may not set dryRun or format (those belong to the batch, which previews, formats and reindexes once), may not nest a batch, and may not two of them resolve to the same file — each entry is planned from its file's pre-edit bytes, so a second entry on one file would discard the first (refused by entry index).

items.description: one edit: `mode` (required: write|update|insert|delete|refactor) plus exactly the options THAT mode accepts at the top level — write takes filePath+content/newContent (+overwrite), update takes symbolName+newContent, insert takes targetSymbolName+newContent (+position), delete takes symbolName (+force), refactor takes symbolName+newName; every entry may also take filePath and lineStart to disambiguate. An option the entry's own mode would not accept at the top level is refused here too, by name, so an entry is validated by the same rule as the single-mode call it mirrors.

files.description: batch only: the fan-out form — each entry applies once per listed project-relative path, and `files` supplies the filePath of every entry (so an entry with `files` must not name its own). Omit it to let each entry name its own target. The list may not repeat a path.

documentation.summary: Unified safe source editing with preview, validation, rollback, and reindex.

returns: Structured mutation result or dry-run preview
Validation, rollback, and reindex status, plus the measured per-file formatter outcome (`formatting`)
Affected paths and caller protection outcomes

`envelope` — the per-file outcome of the call (`planned`, `committed`, `restored`, the pre/post byte counts, and any restore that FAILED with its reason), on the answer and on a refusal alike, so `batch`'s per-file question is answered per file
`batch` (batch only) — one row per `edits` entry with the mode it ran and the files it reached
`importPruning` (delete only) — `attempted`, `language`, the `removedBindings` it removed, and for a language other than TypeScript/JavaScript the `reason` it left the file's imports unchanged
a refusal carries the per-file `envelope` too — the EMPTY one (`entries: []`, nothing committed, nothing restored) with `refusedBeforeWriting: true` when the call refused while planning
errors: Path escape or symlink escape, and a target inside a protected path (`.git/`, `.hg/`, `.svn/`, `node_modules/`, or the index data directory — refused by name before anything is written)
Ambiguous symbol name (the message names filePath/lineStart)
`refactor` onto a name the file already declares, or onto the symbol's current name — both refused at plan time, nothing written
Symbol renamed or removed since the target file was indexed (refreshed first, then refused by name)

`update`, `insert`, `delete` or `refactor` on a project with NO index — the refusal names the reindex command and says that `write` still works, because the symbol modes resolve their target through the index and `write` resolves none
Caller protection, parse, or reindex failure — a FORMATTER failure is not an error: the edit stands and the outcome is reported per file in `formatting` with `formatted: false`

`batch`: an empty or missing `edits`, an entry with no mode or with an option its own mode does not accept (the refusal names the entry index), a per-entry `dryRun`/`format` (they belong to the call), an entry that names its own `filePath` while `files` supplies the targets, a repeated path in `files`, two entries that resolve to ONE file, or more than 200 planned edits — each refused with the run's own reason and nothing written
limitations: Named symbol edits need an INDEX, not a fresh one: when the target file changed after it was indexed, the tool refreshes that ONE file's rows and re-resolves the symbol before planning, so bounds always come from the bytes on disk and never from a stale span. The refresh is reported in `warnings`; if the symbol was renamed or removed in the meantime the edit is refused by name instead of guessing a span

Directly after a write, the file's own evidence is current but cross-file relationships are only re-derived within the bounded post-pass, so a caller in an unrelated file may lag until the next dir index (same bound as bb_index)
Refactoring is identifier-aware static rewriting, not a full language-server proof

Per-mode arguments are enforced in BOTH directions and the accepted set is named, so a rejection can be acted on: `bb_edit update mode does not accept: position (position is accepted for insert) — accepted for update: mode, dryRun, filePath, symbolName, lineStart, content, newContent, format`. An option this mode cannot honor is REFUSED, never silently ignored, and an option that belongs to exactly one other mode says which one. The mode contract: `write` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `filePath`, `content`, `newContent`, `format`, `overwrite`; `update` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `filePath`, `symbolName`, `lineStart`, `content`, `newContent`, `format`; `insert` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `filePath`, `targetSymbolName`, `position`, `lineStart`, `content`, `newContent`, `format`; `delete` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `filePath`, `symbolName`, `lineStart`, `force`, `format`; `refactor` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `filePath`, `symbolName`, `lineStart`, `newName`, `format`; `batch` → `mode`, `dryRun`, `edits`, `files`, `format`.

Body-fragment updates (`newContent` that is a statement, not a declaration) require a BRACE-bodied language. TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, Java, C/C++, Swift, Kotlin, Scala and PHP all take this path. In an indentation- or keyword-delimited language — Python, Ruby, YAML — there is no `{ ... }` range to splice and the tool REFUSES rather than guessing; the refusal names the remedy and passing the full declaration then works. Elixir's `do ... end` is likewise refused. Measured across Python (2-space, 4-space and tab indentation), Ruby at two nesting depths, Go, Rust, Java and Elixir.

`reindexed` is measured from the reindex result, not from the intent: an edit whose reindex reports per-file failures keeps its validated bytes on disk, answers `reindexed: false` and names the files in a `reindex:` warning. The index is then stale for those files; the NEXT symbol edit on them either refreshes that one file inline (when inline refresh is enabled) or refuses with the stale-file remedy (`bb_index` for that file), which is the tool declining to write to bytes it cannot vouch for, not a lost edit.

`delete` refuses when the symbol has indexed callers OR when an import or re-export specifier in another file names it, which covers `import { x as alias }` — the analyzer records no call edge there because it never resolved the alias. The specifier is matched by RESOLVING the module path, not by name, so `../models/user` and `./user` are both caught and a same-named module in a different directory is not. It does NOT refuse for a side-effect-only `import './x'`, a namespace import, or a file with a local that merely shares the name, because none of those can dangle. A forced delete always warns and names every surviving specifier and its file.

KNOWN GAP in `delete`: a tsconfig path alias (`@/models/user`, `~/models/user`) is not caught. The indexer records no import row for a non-relative specifier, so there is nothing to resolve; such a project's only remaining signal is the indexed `calls` edge. A bare package specifier (`react`, `lodash/fp`) is likewise unresolved, correctly, since it cannot be shown to refer to a project file.

Formatting is best-effort and MEASURED, never assumed: an extension with no mapping (`.rb`, `.swift`, `.kt`, `.yaml`, …), a formatter that is not installed, a non-zero exit, and the 1.5s timeout all report `formatted: false` with the per-file reason in `formatting`. The tool never installs a formatter and does not read a project's own formatter configuration — it invokes the standard binary for the extension (prettier/rustfmt/gofmt/clang-format/black-or-ruff) that it can resolve from `node_modules/.bin` or `PATH`.

`write` replacing an existing file is GUARDED rather than free: with `overwrite` omitted, a replacement that removes at least half of the file's lines and at least 5 lines is refused as a probable mistake (a body fragment sent to `write` instead of `update`, or the wrong `filePath`), and the refusal states both line counts, the share that would be lost, and both ways forward. `overwrite: true` replaces it whatever the size; `overwrite: false` is create-only. A 41-line file replaced by one line is therefore refused rather than reported `ok` with nothing distinguishing it from an intentional rewrite

The pre-image check covers staleness on the WRITE side too, and it is not about the index: every target's sha256 is taken as the plan reads it and compared with the bytes the commit is about to replace, immediately before the first write of the batch. A file that changed in that window — an editor saving during a multi-file refactor — is refused with NOTHING written and both hashes named, rather than overwritten from a plan computed against its previous contents. A path the plan intended to create must still not exist; a file that appeared there is refused the same way.

Import cleanup after `delete` is TypeScript/JavaScript-only and AST-driven: the tree names the import statements and identifier occurrences decide usage, so dead bindings are removed and still-used (including aliased and namespace) bindings are kept. In every other language the file is left byte-for-byte unchanged and the answer DECLARES it (`importPruning.attempted: false` with the language and the reason) plus a warning — a leftover import never breaks a build, while an import removed on a pattern can

Writes are refused inside `.git/`, `.hg/`, `.svn/`, `node_modules/`, and the index data directory, by resolved path and by name. That is a safety list beside the security boundary (containment in the project), so a typo'd `filePath` cannot rewrite version-control state or the database the tool's answers come from

A formatter may rewrite a file's line endings with its own: `gofmt -w` turns a CRLF file into LF. The engine restores the file's own ending after formatting and declares the repair on that file's `formatting` entry (`lineEndingRestored: true`), so an edit never silently migrates a file to another line-ending convention

A commit is SECONDS, not milliseconds: it formats, validates and reindexes synchronously before answering. Measured warm p50/p95 on lane fixtures: update commit 1801.5/2062.9 ms on a 5-file fixture and 4500.7/7052.3 ms on a 100-file fixture; a dry run of the same edit is 11.5-71 ms p50. The MCP client's 30 s timeout is the only ceiling, and a timed-out write call is the case where `envelope` (or a re-run, which re-plans against the current bytes) is how a caller recovers committed-versus-restored
tools.performance: Only affected files are written, formatted, validated and reindexed; work is proportional to the TOUCHED file, not the project size. A missing formatter costs no subprocess at all: the binary is resolved before anything is spawned. `batch` pays each step ONCE for the whole call (one formatting pass, one validation pass, one reindex), and dry runs plan only: measured p50/p95 on lane fixtures, an update dry run is 11.5/11.8 ms on a 5-file fixture and 71.0/76.8 ms on a 100-file fixture, while a commit of the same edit is 1801.5/2062.9 ms and 4500.7/7052.3 ms respectively because it also formats, validates and reindexes before answering
tools.safety: Write-capable. Uses project-root path checks, atomic writes, snapshots, validation, and rollback; use dryRun before risky edits. dryRun writes no source file, but a stale target file is still refreshed in the INDEX first (derived data only), because the bounds it previews must be the bounds the real edit would use. `write` on an existing file is guarded against the catastrophic case — a replacement that removes at least half of a file's lines and at least 5 lines needs `overwrite: true`, and `overwrite: false` makes the write create-only — and every committed batch re-checks that the bytes it is replacing are the bytes the plan read, refusing with nothing written when they moved. The guard's refusal is raised at PLAN time, so a dry run reports exactly what the real call would. `batch` plans every entry before the first write, so a refusal anywhere is a refusal of the whole call; the pre-image check then reads every target of the call at once — a target that moved refuses all of it, including entries whose own plan was fine; and a failure AFTER the writes restores each committed file and reports what happened in `envelope` rather than in one boolean. Two entries that resolve to one file are refused rather than composed, because both are planned from that file's pre-edit bytes.
tools.evidence: Mutation bounds come from indexed AST bytes, re-resolved from the file on disk whenever the indexed rows are stale; validation and reindex state report whether post-edit evidence is current. The plan's own pre-images are checked against disk immediately before the write, so a plan is applied only to the bytes it was computed from. `write` is the one mode that consumes no indexed row: it takes its bytes from the request and the disk, which is why it is also the one mode usable on a project with no index.

tools.name: bb_index
tools.description: Reindex a file or directory so the index reflects edits immediately (agent-fresh). Accepts a path (file or dir); a file reindexes only that file, a dir runs an incremental index of that dir (changed files only). mode=post re-runs the heavy derived-data phases (relationships/enrichment/gravity/taints/health) WITHOUT re-parsing — the remediation after edits on incremental paths. Every mode requires `path`, and it MUST resolve inside this project: an absolute path elsewhere, a `../` traversal, a foreign directory and a symlink inside the project pointing out of it are all REFUSED, because an out-of-tree file would be stored with a `relative_path` that is not relative to anything and every scoped query, file name and freshness check for it would then be wrong. For mode=post the path must additionally NOT be a file: the phases are project-wide, so pass the project root (or a directory inside it). The report says what happened rather than only how much: `outcome` is `indexed`, `partial` or `no-op`; a no-op carries a `reason` that distinguishes "nothing changed: the file already matches the index (mtime, size and sha256 agree)" from "this file holds nothing the indexer extracts", and `unchanged`/`declined`/`skipped` say how many files fell into each case. When errors occurred, `errorDetail` names the file and the message beside the `errors` count, and `walCheckpointed` says whether the write WAL was reclaimed after the run. Paths in the report are PROJECT-RELATIVE, so the same request returns the same bytes on any machine. The counts are stable between identical calls; the `ms` fields are measured wall-clock and are expected to vary.

path.description: Project-relative file (reindex only that file) or directory (incremental index of changed files); for mode=post, the project root or a directory inside it whose derived phases should be re-run (a file path is refused). REQUIRED in every mode and checked rather than ignored. Must resolve INSIDE the project: both sides are resolved through realpath, so a symlink inside the project pointing out of it is refused too.

mode.description: auto (default) infers file vs dir from path; file reindexes one file (unchanged files answer no-op instead of being re-parsed); dir runs an incremental directory index; post re-runs derived phases (relationships/taints/health) without re-parsing

documentation.summary: Immediately refresh the index for a just-written/edited file or directory; mode=post re-derives relationships/taints/health without re-parsing.

returns: `indexed`, `deleted`, `errors`, `unchanged`, `declined` and `skipped` counts for the refreshed path
The mode actually applied (`auto` resolves to `file` or `dir`; `file`/`dir`/`post` are reported as named)

`outcome` — `indexed`, `partial`, or `no-op`. A no-op also carries `reason`, and the two reasons are different facts: "nothing changed" (mtime, size and sha256 all still match the stored row) versus "this file holds nothing the indexer extracts" (an extension the indexer does not parse)
`errorDetail`: the file and the message for each failure, beside the `errors` count
`walCheckpointed`: whether the write-ahead log was reclaimed after the run (a refused checkpoint — another reader holding a snapshot — reports false, never success)
For mode=dir, `candidates` (files the walk found changed) beside `processed`, so a partial dir index is visible as a count, and `unchanged: true` when the tree is settled

For mode=post, the per-phase report (relationships, enrichment, gravity, taint, health, integrity, planner stats, vector blobs, analysis) with each phase's timing and outcome, `totalMs`, and the post-run `integrityHealth` score
errors: Missing or blank path
A path that resolves OUTSIDE the project — an absolute path elsewhere, a `../` traversal, a foreign directory, or a symlink inside the project pointing out of it — for file, dir, auto AND post mode
mode=post with a path that does not exist, or with a FILE path: the post pass re-derives project-wide phases, so it takes the project root (or a directory inside it)
mode=file on a directory, or mode=dir on a file
Unknown mode, or an option this tool does not accept (the refusal names the accepted set)

Another LIVE indexer holding the project lock; the refusal names the holder's pid, host and start time, and the remedy. A lock whose holder is dead, a lock naming no process once it is older than the grace window, and a foreign-host lock past its 24h expiry are reclaimed automatically
limitations: A file reindex updates only that file's evidence; cross-file relationships are repaired within the bounded post-pass for the touched files (see `derived.pass`), while callers in unrelated files can lag until the next dir or full index

Dir mode reuses the incremental indexer: unchanged files are skipped by design, a settled tree answers `unchanged: true`, and a file the walk's skip rules exclude is left untouched in the index rather than being treated as deleted — an index row is deleted only when the file is genuinely gone from disk

File mode's `no-op` is a real no-op: an unchanged file is detected by mtime+size and confirmed by comparing the stored sha256 with the bytes on disk, so a repeated call does not re-parse (and does not pay a parse's latency)
The COUNTS in a report are stable between identical calls; the `ms` fields are measured wall-clock and DO vary, so a diff of two reports will show timing drift

Dir mode walks with the indexer's own skip rules; a directory that the indexer excludes from DISCOVERY (build output, dependency trees) is not revisited by an incremental dir walk. The walk's skip list matches discovery's for the names that matter here — `vendor` is indexed, because it is first-party source in Go and in repositories that curate code under src/vendor
A reindex does not run the full derived pipeline: `derived.pass` is `bounded` for incremental runs, and mode=post is the explicit remedy when derived data looks stale
tools.performance: A single-file reindex is bounded by that file's parse cost plus the incremental post-pass; dir mode is bounded by the changed-file set and reports how many candidates it found against how many it processed. A no-op refresh (unchanged file or settled directory) performs no parse at all. Measured on an isolated tiny fixture, a warm file-mode call was 11.8 s when it always re-parsed and 0.0 s–0.1 s as a no-op; the parse path is dominated by worker-pool startup, not the file.
tools.safety: Write-capable against INDEX data only — it never modifies source files, and it never deletes an index row for a file that still exists on disk. It will only index paths inside this project: both sides are resolved through realpath, so a symlink inside the project pointing out of it is refused and a symlink to a file inside it is allowed. Concurrent index runs are refused by the project index lock rather than interleaved.
tools.evidence: Counts come from the real parse/store pipeline. The report's own assertions are checked by the m40 A1/A3 gates (post entry, write-path parity including the delete guard and the unchanged-file no-op), m43 P1 (lock), m22 E1/D3 (agent-fresh), and by real MCP stdio door probes under validation/tools/bb_index/.

tools.name: bb_graph
tools.description: Per-symbol dependency graph over the canonical graph engine: callers, callees, per-edge evidence tier (structural/import_based/usage_contextual/reference_qualified/inferred), the stored evidence class and resolution basis behind each tier, confidence, and cross-language edge count. Same engine and tier rules the editor graph panel uses; truncated traversals are declared with a reason, never silent. Traversal semantics: a relationship stored against any member of a class (a method call, an inherited behavior) is attributed to the owner class, so caller/callee sets include the owner-family level — every edge still traces to a stored relationship row and states whether it matched the symbol itself or one of its members. Each edge's `rowId` is the stored relationship key with its leading '<projectHash>:rel:' removed, and each endpoint's `id` is the stored symbol key with its leading '<projectHash>:' removed — both prefixes are constant within one answer, and `root.id` carries the FULL stored form, so '<projectHash>' is the segment before its first ':' and prepending it (plus ':rel:' for a rowId) reconstructs the store key exactly. An `ext:` id has no such prefix and is returned whole. The graph is READ from a read-only index handle: asking a question cannot mutate the index. Measured on this repository's reference index (11,440 files, 310,423 symbols, 820,040 stored relationships), a default call answers in 22-355 ms p95 depending on the symbol's degree, where the same call took 131 s before the engine's cascade and arm queries were rewritten to seek their indexes.

symbol.description: symbol name to root the graph at (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases). Required; a blank name is refused as missing. An unknown name is refused after the resolver's declared containment fallback runs: that fallback is a substring scan, and on the 11,440-file reference index it costs about 5 s before answering not-found. It is a documented step of the resolver, not a silent budget breach; an exact-name miss does not run it.

maxDepth.description: traversal depth bound (default 5, max 10). Must be a whole number: a fractional depth is refused rather than floored.

direction.description: which side to traverse (default both). 'callers' answers "who depends on this" and skips the callee walk entirely — on a real index that is the difference between 1 edge and 37 in the same payload.

relationshipTypes.description: stored relationship kinds to include. Default: EVERY kind the index stores (calls, extends, implements, uses, instantiates, overrides, contains, references, imports, exports, decorates, renders, mixes_in, part_of) — deliberately not narrowed, because a narrower default silently drops a fifth of the graph and cannot descend a class hierarchy: 'contains' is the parent-to-member edge, so excluding it means a traversal rooted at a class cannot reach that class's own methods. The cost is size — the type-level 'uses'/'references'/'contains' rows are roughly half of what a typical index stores, so a hub symbol's default answer is 2.5-4.8x larger than a filtered one (measured: lodash 487 KiB against 101 KiB, ripgrep 795 against 321). Pass relationshipTypes: ['calls'] for the pure call graph, or ['implements'] to see only interface satisfaction. A kind you do not list is never reported; a filter you supply is a REQUEST, not a bound — it is reported in `summary.filterNarrowed` and `summary.filterReason` (never in `truncationReason`, which is reserved for bounds), and the kinds actually searched come back in `summary.scope.relationshipTypes`.

includeCrossLanguage.description: include edges the indexer marked cross-language (default true). Set false for a single-language view; the rows removed BY REQUEST are counted in `summary.crossLanguageExcluded` per direction, so an empty set beside a non-zero count is a request, not an empty store.

timeBudgetMs.description: wall-clock ceiling for the whole walk in milliseconds. DEFAULT 0 = NO clock bound: every other bound on this answer is a function of the DATA (edgeLimit, the 50-symbol per-direction fan-out, maxEdges, maxDepth), so the default answer is complete over them and byte-identical on a re-run. Pass a value only to cap latency, and know what you are buying: the ceiling is checked BETWEEN statements and never inside one — a SQLite statement cannot be interrupted — so a run that hits it returns a SAMPLE of the set. The sample is declared, never silent: `summary.timeBudgetExhausted` is true and `walk-time-budget-exhausted` is among `summary.truncationReasons`. There is no value that makes a clock-bounded answer reproducible; if you need the whole set, leave this unset

maxEdges.description: hard cap on the number of edges in the WHOLE answer, across both directions and all depths (default 1000, max 5000; whole numbers only). `edgeLimit` bounds one query and this bounds the answer; their product is what a caller receives. Reaching it is declared as `total-edge-limit` with the value in `summary.maxEdges`. Raise it for a hub symbol, lower it for a quick shape check — a value below `edgeLimit` IS honored (the answer stops at it and says so), so `maxEdges` is the knob for "just show me the shape"

edgeLimit.description: Per-symbol call-site limit for one edge query (default 200, max 5000; whole numbers only). Reaching it is declared in `summary.truncated` with `summary.truncationReason` and the root's true count in `summary.callersIfUncapped`/`summary.calleesIfUncapped` — the limit is never a silent cap. Raise it to receive more sites in one answer.

documentation.summary: Per-symbol graph with per-edge evidence tiers — the agent view of the editor's graph panel.

returns: Per-symbol dependency graph: callers and callees
Per-edge endpoints as described nodes — `{ id, name, symbolType, file, line, isExternal }` on BOTH ends, so an edge is self-contained and no id has to be parsed or looked up in a second call

Per-edge `rowId`: the stored `brain_relationship` row the edge came from, so every claim is auditable against the index (measured: every emitted rowId resolves to exactly one stored row, and the edge's endpoints agree with that row)
Endpoints the index could not resolve as `ext:<name>` nodes, with `isExternal: true` — a recorded name, never a symbol guessed from that name

Per-edge `match` (`exact` | `owner-cascade`) and `matchedMember` (`{ name, file }` when the cascade matched): whether the stored row names the symbol that was asked for, or one of its members folded onto it

Per-edge `evidenceClass`: the stored classification when the index made one, or `null` when the `tier` was DERIVED from the edge's own stored kind and confidence — so a reader can tell a stored claim from a derivation without a second query

Per-edge `targetBasis`: why the target may claim this identity, from the stored row — `symbol` (a stored declaration), `external` or `unresolved` (a name the index could not attach). Never inferred by this tool
Per-edge evidence tier (structural/import_based/usage_contextual/reference_qualified/inferred) with confidence

Per-edge call-site address: `{ kind, file, line, note }` — `call-site` is an exact stored line; `declaration` is a LABELED substitute (the calling symbol's own declaration, shown only when no call-site line is stored); `unknown` has no position at all (line null) and states why. A position is never fabricated and never reported as line 0

`summary.edgesByType`: the composition of the RETURNED edges by stored relationship kind, counted from the emitted edges. The default filter covers every stored kind, so an answer is usually not all call edges — measured: lodash `baseConvert` 99 of 230, cobra `getCompletions` 36 of 65, rake `standard_rake_options` 72 of 76. This is how you learn the ratio without walking the edges

`summary.maxEdges` / `totalEdgeLimitReached`: the bound on the WHOLE answer, across both directions and every depth, and whether it bit. `edgeLimit` bounds one query; this bounds the answer, and their product is what a caller receives. A requested `maxEdges` is HONORED even below `edgeLimit` — `{maxEdges: 5}` returns 5 edges with `totalEdgeLimitReached: true` and `truncationReason: "total-edge-limit"` — so it is the way to ask for a quick shape check

`summary.truncated` / `truncationReason` / `truncationReasons`: a DECLARED BOUND bit — the walk stopped before the store ran out. `truncationReasons` is the same set as a list (`truncationReason` is its `+`-joined rendering, kept for existing consumers)

`summary.filterNarrowed` / `filterReason`: the `relationshipTypes` argument narrowed the QUESTION — a request, not a bound. `filterNarrowed: true` with `truncated: false` means the edge sets are the whole of what was asked for (and possibly not the whole of what the store holds); `filterReason` names the narrowing (e.g. `relationshipTypes:calls|uses`) and is `null` when the default kind set ran. Asking for `relationshipTypes:["implements"]` on a symbol with none answers 0 edges with `truncated: false, filterNarrowed: true` — an empty subset, not a clipped answer

`summary.edgeKindPriority`: the order in which kinds survive the per-symbol site limit — dependency kinds first, then lexical, then module-level, then membership. Only observable under `truncated`, published always

`summary.scope.relationshipTypes`: the relationship kinds this run actually searched, RESOLVED from the engine's own registered list rather than restated, so the filter that produced the answer is never a restatement of a default that may have moved

`summary.exactCallers` / `cascadedCallers` / `exactCallees` / `cascadedCallees`: DEPTH 0 only — how much of the answer is about the symbol that was asked for and how much the owner cascade folded in from its members. `deeperCallers` / `deeperCallees` hold the edges about symbols the traversal discovered, so exact + cascaded + deeper is the number of edges returned

`summary.callerBudget` / `calleeBudget` with `callerBudgetExhausted` / `calleeBudgetExhausted`: the fan-out bound in force and whether it bit. `truncationReason` can name `caller-budget-exhausted`; this says what the budget was

`summary.unattributed`: stored rows that NAME this symbol (or one of its owner-cascade members) but carry no source symbol, so the caller and callee queries — which join the source side — cannot show them in either direction. Per direction, depth 0 only, and `null` (not zero) when the count could not be taken. Measured on this repository's index: 11.0% of stored rows (69,171 of 631,139) carry no source symbol and 2,099 symbols answered `callers: []` while the store held incoming rows for them. The rows are counted, never fabricated into edges

`summary.noiseFiltered` and `summary.crossLanguageExcluded`: how many stored rows this answer dropped BY POLICY (vendored, generated, fixture, snapshot, dist or build paths, and generated names) and BY REQUEST (`includeCrossLanguage: false`), per direction. Both are filters, not bounds: `truncated` stays false while they bite, which is why they are numbers rather than prose — a zero edge set beside a non-zero count is a policy or a request, not an empty result
`summary.edgesInBothDirections`: stored rows present in both the caller and the callee list — `totalCallers + totalCallees` double-counts exactly this many

`root.candidates` and `root.match`: how many stored symbols the requested name resolved among, and which resolution step won — `exact`, `exact-any-kind` (the name is a symbol the graph cannot traverse: a constant, a type alias), or `containment` (the answer is about a symbol whose name CONTAINS the one asked for, so the name was not itself a symbol). When `root.candidates` is greater than 1 the graph is about one of those symbols, so confirm `root` first

`summary.maxDepth` and `summary.maxDepthReached`: the bound this run actually used and the depth it actually reached. Together they are the only way to tell "the walk finished" from "the walk stopped"
A per-edge `depth`, which is HOW FAR THE WALK WENT before finding that row — not the shortest distance between two symbols. See Limitations

`summary.scope`: the `direction`, `relationshipTypes` and `includeCrossLanguage` actually applied, so a narrowed traversal returning zero edges is distinguishable from a widened one that found nothing
Declared truncation with a reason when the traversal is bounded
errors: Missing symbol (a blank/whitespace-only `symbol` is refused as missing, not echoed back)
`maxDepth` outside the declared 1-10 range, or not a whole number
`edgeLimit` outside 1-5000, or not a whole number
`maxEdges` outside 1-5000, or not a whole number
`direction` outside `callers`|`callees`|`both`
`relationshipTypes` given as an empty list, or with a blank entry (a narrowed traversal that can match nothing is refused rather than silently reinterpreted)
`timeBudgetMs` negative (0 is accepted and means no clock bound)
`includeCrossLanguage` not a boolean
An option the tool does not accept (the acceptance set and the aliases are named in the error)

Symbol not found in the index. The refusal runs the resolver's three declared steps first — exact name among traversable kinds, exact name among all kinds, then a `LIKE '%name%'` containment fallback — and the containment step is a substring scan: on the 11,440-file reference index an unknown name costs about 5 s before the not-found error. That cost is the declared fallback, not a hidden budget breach, and it is the same step that lets a near-miss (`root.match: "containment"`) answer instead of refusing
limitations: Edges reflect indexed static evidence with declared tiers; inferred edges are labeled, not proven

An edge's `depth` is the depth of the query that found its stored row, not the shortest path between the two symbols. The traversal is depth-first and the per-row dedupe is global, so the first traversal to reach a row emits it: measured, 24% of edges on cobra, 57% on lodash and 60% on rake sit deeper than the shortest path in their own answer. No edge ever claims a SHORTER path than its answer can demonstrate, so `depth` is a valid upper bound on distance — read it as 'how far the walk got', not 'how far apart these are'. Use `direction` with a smaller `maxDepth` when the distance itself matters

The default filter covers every stored relationship kind, so an answer mixes dependency edges with lexical references (`uses`, `references`), structural membership (`contains`) and module edges (`imports`, `exports`). `contains` means owner → member: a class reporting its own methods is structure, not dependency. Filter with `relationshipTypes` for a pure call graph, or read `edgesByType`

Every kind competes for the per-symbol site limit, and the surviving set is decided by `edgeKindPriority` — dependency kinds first. A truncated answer therefore keeps more `calls` and fewer `contains` than an untruncated one would, and the published order is the rule that decides it

A target the index could not resolve appears as an `ext:<name>` node rather than as a symbol. That is a real gap in the index, surfaced rather than papered over: the edge `caller --calls--> ext:name` is what the store holds, and no internal symbol is substituted for it

A blank or whitespace-only `symbol` is refused immediately (it used to be sent through the containment scan and echoed back in the not-found message). An unknown name is refused AFTER the containment fallback runs, which scans symbol names: about 5 s on the 11,440-file reference index. Both refusals are declared here because a caller budgeting latency on this tool should not discover the scan from a timeout

The graph reflects the index as of the last index run. This tool does not auto-refresh and does not report per-file staleness; when files changed after indexing, run: bb index --changed (or the `bb_index` tool with the project path)

Owner-cascade attribution: a relationship stored against a class member (e.g. a call to a method) is reported toward the owner class, so caller/callee sets are a superset of exact-symbol-only matches. The superset is REDUCIBLE: every edge carries `match` (`exact` or `owner-cascade`), `matchedMember` naming the member the stored row actually referenced, and the summary carries the exact/cascade split. Measured on cobra, `Command` (182 methods) answers with 184 caller edges of which 24 name `Command` itself. Every edge also carries the `rowId` it traces to

A target the index could not resolve is reported as an `ext:<name>` node — a NAME the index saw and could not attach to a symbol — and is never resolved by matching that name against other symbols in the project. The name is not unique there (measured on vscode, `match` names 37,876 stored symbols; on svelte, `end` names 437,570), so matching it would manufacture edges the store does not contain, crowd out the resolvable callees, and seed the traversal with a guess. `ext:` nodes are leaves: there is nothing stored about them to walk into

Two identical calls return identical answers: the DEFAULT asks for no wall-clock bound, and every remaining bound — the per-query site limit, the fan-out budget, the total-answer bound, the depth — is a function of the data. Passing `timeBudgetMs` ends that guarantee on purpose: the ceiling is checked BETWEEN statements and never inside one (a SQLite statement is not interruptible), so a run that hits it returns a declared SAMPLE of the set — `summary.timeBudgetExhausted: true` with `walk-time-budget-exhausted` among `summary.truncationReasons`

A symbol name is not a unique identifier. When one name matches several stored symbols the resolver takes the highest-gravity match (ties broken by lowest id, so the pick is reproducible rather than SQLite's whim) and says how many it chose between in `root.candidates` — measured: `build` in lodash resolves among 7, `code_block.go` in cobra among 50, `Command` among 1. When `root.candidates` is greater than 1 the graph is about ONE of those symbols, so confirm `root` is the one you meant before reading the edges. The other candidates are not listed

A name containing a SQL LIKE wildcard (`%`, `_`) is matched LITERALLY, not as a pattern: it either resolves to a symbol that genuinely contains those characters or is reported not found. It never widens into a match on an unrelated symbol

Call-site positions depend on the analyzer: an exact line is claimed only where the index stored a real line; a legacy 0 or a NULL line yields the declared `declaration` or `unknown` address instead (derived by src/intelligence/graph/line-address.ts — never an inline fallback)

`summary.totalCallers`/`totalCallees` are the RETURNED counts, not the totals. A per-symbol site limit (`edgeLimit`, default 200, max 5000) bounds one edge query; when it is reached the answer declares `truncated` with `truncationReason` naming the bound (`caller-site-limit` / `callee-site-limit`), `cappedQueries` says how many queries hit it, and `callersIfUncapped`/`calleesIfUncapped` carry the root's true site count (null when no cap was reached — never zero). The cap fires only when rows were ACTUALLY dropped: the query asks for one row beyond the limit, so a symbol holding exactly `edgeLimit` sites is reported complete instead of falsely truncated

An empty caller or callee set is not proof that nothing references the symbol. Three populations sit BESIDE the edge sets rather than inside them, each with its own number: rows the JOIN cannot attribute because they carry no source symbol (`summary.unattributed`), rows removed by the noise policy (`summary.noiseFiltered`), and rows removed by the `includeCrossLanguage: false` scope option (`summary.crossLanguageExcluded`). Read them before concluding that a set is empty — in the measured index one symbol had 40 stored `calls` rows and answered three callers, 38 of them in the first population

`truncated` means a BOUND bit, and nothing else. A `relationshipTypes` filter does not set it: the filter reports through `summary.filterNarrowed` / `filterReason` instead. The two questions are separate and both are answerable — "is this the whole store?" (`truncated`) and "is this the whole of what I asked for?" (`filterNarrowed` + the counts)

`provenance.evidenceClass` is `inferred` for the ANSWER, not for every edge: root resolution (a gravity tie-break, or the containment fallback), the owner cascade, the noise policy and any cap are constructions over stored rows, so the whole object cannot claim `structural` even when each returned edge carries one stored row. Per-row evidence is on each edge's `tier` (a stored `calls` row is `structural`) and its `evidenceClass` / `targetBasis`
tools.performance: maxDepth (default 5, max 10) bounds traversal; per-edge evidence resolution is bounded by the returned subgraph. The answer is bounded at four levels and every level is declared: the per-query site limit (`edgeLimit`, default 200, max 5000), the fan-out budget (50 symbols per direction, `callerBudget`/`calleeBudget`), the size of the WHOLE answer (`maxEdges`, default 1000, max 5000) and the depth. The third exists because the product of the first two is not a number a reader can use: measured, ripgrep's `unwrap` returns 206 edges at depth 1, 454 at depth 3 and 702 at depth 5 — 228 KiB, 504 KiB and 770 KiB rendered. Reaching `maxEdges` is declared as `total-edge-limit` with the value in `summary.maxEdges`, and a `maxEdges` below `edgeLimit` is honored rather than raised to it (`{maxEdges: 5}` answers 5 edges, `totalEdgeLimitReached: true`). The wall-clock ceiling (`timeBudgetMs`) is OFF BY DEFAULT (0): it is the ONE bound here that is a function of the clock rather than of the data, so it is the caller's decision, never the tool's — and it is checked between statements, never inside one, so a run that hits it returns a declared SAMPLE (`timeBudgetExhausted`, `walk-time-budget-exhausted`) rather than a bounded latency. Measured on this repository's reference index (11,440 files, 310,423 symbols, 820,040 stored relationships): a default call on a leaf symbol answers in 22 ms p50 / 30 ms p95, a mid symbol with 307 edges in 161 ms / 355 ms, and a hub with 672 callers in 90 ms / 125 ms. Those numbers are 4,000-6,000x faster than the same calls before the engine's cascade and arm queries were rewritten to seek their indexes (a leaf default call was 131 s p50, and mid/hub default calls did not answer inside ten minutes), and the traversal now opens the index read-only, so a question never mutates the index (open cost 19.6 ms, down from 18,714 ms for the read-write open). The engine reference (docs/GRAPH_ENGINE.md) carries the statement-level before/after and the plan shapes that hold it.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data: the traversal opens the index read-only, with no migrations, no auto-refresh and no write tool. When the index is stale, refresh it deliberately with: bb index --changed (or the bb_index tool with the project path).
tools.evidence: Nodes and edges come from the canonical graph engine over brain_symbol and brain_relationship rows; each edge carries its evidence tier, the stored classification that may have decided it (`evidenceClass`), the stored resolution basis of its target (`targetBasis`), its confidence, the `rowId` of the row it came from, and `match`/`matchedMember` saying whether the row names the traced symbol or one of its members. Every emitted rowId resolves to exactly one stored row and the edge's endpoints agree with that row. The declared totals are counted with the same query and the same noise filters as the returned edges, so a reported total is the number a caller would receive if no limit existed. Owner-cascade edges are auditable in the same way: `match` and `matchedMember` identify the member the stored row actually named, and the exact/cascade split in the summary is verified against an independent SQL count of direct-target rows on real repos (cobra: tool reports `exactCallers: 24`; oracle counts 24 direct caller rows for the same symbol). The traversal's row sets were compared before and after the query-plan rewrite over a leaf, three classes with 3-6 members, a 143-callee mid symbol and a 672-caller hub: identical rowIds for both arms and both unattributed counts (validation/tools/bb_graph/results/semantics-equivalence.json).

tools.name: bb_impact
tools.description: Bounded reverse-dependency impact for one symbol via the same component the editor graph panel uses: declared node budget (200) and depth (5), truncation as a first-class field with reason, and a declared total that is the size of the set the answer is a prefix of — measured, not inferred, so an answer that is short of the whole set says so even when no bound fired. Unknown symbols are loud declared errors — an empty impact set is never invented. Owner-cascade applies: impact includes dependents attributed at class level, not only exact-symbol rows. The relationship kinds that count are named in every answer's `rule.relationshipTypes` and can be overridden; a dependent carries its evidence tier, cross-language flag, bridge and position.

symbol.description: symbol name to compute impact for (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

relationshipTypes.description: stored relationship kinds to count as dependencies. Default: calls, instantiates, extends, implements. A kind that is not listed is never reported, and the applied list is echoed in `rule.relationshipTypes` on every answer. This is the same control bb_graph has, so a caller who wants the type-level `uses`/`references` rows can ask for them on either door.

file.description: optional defining-file hint for a symbol NAME that several stored symbols carry — the same server-resolved identity the editor's hover sends as `file`. Accept the stored project-relative path, or an absolute path ending in it. It must identify the symbol: a hint that does not is REFUSED with a named error, never silently ignored and never silently relabelled to another same-named copy. Ambiguous MEMBER names (constructors, members outside the graph's root types) resolve through their owning declaration at the hinted file; for a traversable name the walk roots where the graph engine resolves it, and a hint naming another copy is refused rather than answered. Omit it for unique names.

refresh.description: set false to skip the bounded staleness repair and answer from the existing index. When omitted, stale files inside the answer are repaired and the walk is re-run so the answer is not built from the rows the refresh replaced.

documentation.summary: Bounded impact with declared truncation — identical numbers to the editor's impact mode.

returns: The rule the answer was MEASURED under, in `rule`: which relationship kinds count as dependencies (the applied list is echoed here on every answer), the owner-cascade, the noise policy, and the depth cap. The set and the declared total are measurements of this same list

The declared limits, from the component that owns them: `budget` (node budget 200, depth cap 5, and the three ceilings the declared total is computed under) and `traversal` (depth actually reached, the engine's own truncation state and reason, its per-query site limit, its capped-query count, and the root's uncapped caller count when computable). `maxDepth` is an EXPANSION cap: direct dependents are `depth: 0`, so the deepest dependent the engine can report is `maxDepth - 1` (4), and the depth cap is shared by the completeness measurement, so a declared total is the total UNDER that cap

Whether the set is the WHOLE truth or a prefix of a larger one, and how that was established: whenever truncation was declared or the walk reached the last expandable depth, the returned set is measured against an unbounded walk of the same rule, and a prefix is declared when the two disagree. `countVerification` carries `ran`, `timedOut`, `boundarySuspect` and `complete` — `complete: true` means the measurement proved the returned set IS the whole truth (an ENGINE row cap may still have fired on the way; it is then published in `traversal.engineTruncated`, because a row cap that dropped only duplicate call sites of an already-counted dependent hides no dependent), `false` means a prefix or a declared unknown, and `null` means no measurement was bought because the set is complete by construction (shallow walk, no bound fired)

Downstream dependents of the symbol with per-edge evidence tiers and confidence, cross-language flags, bridge mechanism, and each dependent's own position. Every one of those describes ONE stored row, and `evidenceAtDepth` says which path that row is on: `depth` is the MEASURED shortest path, while the graph engine walks depth-first and stamps the first trace, so the two can name different rows (measured across nine repositories before this was fixed: 340 of 4 258 rows, 7.98%). The evidence is re-read at the reported depth, and where no row can be attributed every evidence field is null rather than quoted from a longer path

How the requested name became the root it walked: `rootMatch` carries the name asked for, whether the match was exact, an `exact-exempt-kind` hit (the name matched EXACTLY and unambiguously but the kind — an enum variant, a constant, a plain field — is outside the graph whitelist, so the walk is the one every other root gets and nothing was substituted), a containment match, or the member→owner substitution, and how many stored symbols carry that exact name. An ambiguous traversable name is ANSWERED about the copy the engine resolves, with `rootMatch.nameMatches` disclosing the ambiguity; an ambiguous member name is refused unless a `file` hint identifies its owning declaration

How each dependent is a dependent, per row, in `via`: `exact` (the stored row names the symbol asked about), `member` (it names one of its members — the owner cascade working as declared, with the member named in `viaMember`), or `range-folded` (it names neither, and the row is in the answer only because the cascade RANGE widened). `cascade` is the composition of the returned set by those three, or `null` when the index refused the member lookups it needs to establish it

`directCount` — the number of DIRECT dependents (depth 0), or `null` when the completeness measurement hit a declared ceiling, was refused, or stopped on its clock. `totalCountIfKnown` is the transitive total under the same rule, or `null` for the same declared unknowns. Neither is ever smaller than `shownCount`; when the measurement proves the set complete they equal it

`file` — an optional defining-file hint for a name several stored symbols carry. For a member name (a constructor, or a member the graph cannot root) it resolves the walk through the MEMBER'S OWNING DECLARATION at that file and the result says so in `resolution`. For a traversable name the walk roots where the graph engine resolves the name, and the hint is a REFUSAL input: it either identifies that copy or the answer is a named error, never a silent relabel to another copy

Freshness: a per-dependent `stale` flag (`true`/`false`, or `null` when the file is not in the index at all) and a summary `freshness` envelope; `rootStale` declares the root's own file separately, since a stale root with fresh dependents is still a stale answer. Stale files inside the answer are repaired within budget and the walk is re-run, declared in `autoRefresh`; `refresh=false` opts out

Loud declared errors instead of fabricated empty sets: an unknown symbol, an ambiguous member name with no usable hint, a hint that does not identify the symbol, an empty `relationshipTypes` list, and the option refusals the shared validator raises are all named errors with `isError` set
errors: Missing symbol
Symbol not found in the index — a declared error, never an empty impact set that would read as "nothing depends on this"

The requested NAME is an ambiguous MEMBER name (a constructor or a kind outside the graph's root types) and no usable `file` hint was given. The error lists the candidate copies with file and line (bounded to 8, plus a count of the rest) and names the `file` option as the remediation

A `file` hint that does not identify the symbol — an unknown path, or a path naming a different copy than the symbol the walk would root at — is refused with a named error instead of being ignored or answered about another copy
`relationshipTypes` given as an empty list: refused rather than silently re-read as the engine's default kind set (an empty rule matches nothing, and the engine would substitute its default)

The root resolves to a non-traversable kind AND is not the symbol that was asked for — a gravity pick, a containment match, or a re-root through an owner. The graph whitelist exists so a request is never answered about a DIFFERENT symbol, and that is the only case left where it applies
An option this tool does not accept, or a value of the wrong type, is rejected by the shared tool validator with the accepted options named
limitations: Static impact analysis cannot establish runtime behavior: it reads stored relationship rows, not executed calls

The depth cap is an EXPANSION cap. Direct dependents are `depth: 0`, the deepest reported dependent is `maxDepth - 1` (4), and the completeness measurement shares that cap — so a declared total is the total under the declared depth, and a chain deeper than the cap keeps a declared `caller-depth-cap-reached` truncation rather than claiming a bounded set is the whole truth

The engine's row bounds are not truncations of the DEPENDENT SET: a per-query call-site limit, a per-traversal caller budget and a total-edge cap drop ROWS. When the measurement proves the returned set complete, those bounds stay visible in `traversal.engineTruncated` / `engineTruncationReason` and `truncated` stays false — the set is whole even though the engine stopped emitting rows

When the completeness measurement cannot finish — 50 000 scanned rows, 2 000 expansions, or its own 4 000 ms circuit breaker — `totalCountIfKnown` and `directCount` are BOTH `null` (a declared unknown). The clock is the one bound that is a property of the machine rather than the index; when it fires, `reproducible: false` is published and the truncation reason names it

The graph engine applies NO wall-clock bound to the caller walk unless a caller asks for one, so this tool's walk is bounded by the index itself. What can still make two identical calls differ is the completeness measurement's own circuit breaker, which is published rather than hidden

Latency depends on the index's own planner state as well as on the size of the database: the walk's per-symbol caller query must be planned through the owner-range and target indexes to stay index-bounded. On the current reference index it is (per-symbol p95 153.6–327.7 ms, measured byte-read-only); an earlier campaign measurement on a pre-fix index state returned multi-second-to-minute answers and is retained in the evidence as the reason the owner-range index exists. The fixture tiers are the regression baselines (see Performance)

Owner-cascade attribution applies: dependents through class-member relationships are attributed to the owner class. The cascade RANGE is a strict SUPERSET of the owner relation — it never loses a dependent the owner relation has, but it folds in siblings of a member: ripgrep `RegexMatcher` answered 21 dependents of which 7 were `range-folded` and 0 were real members. `cascade.rangeFolded` counts those rows, so the over-count is visible instead of silent

A `file` hint cannot select a DIFFERENT copy of a traversable name: the graph engine roots by name (gravity-ordered), and the hint can only confirm that copy or refuse. Member names are the case the hint resolves, through their owning declaration

`relationshipTypes` is not validated against the index's stored-kind vocabulary: a misspelled kind is measured as an empty set with `truncated: false`, and `rule.relationshipTypes` echoes the misspelling so the mistake is auditable rather than disguised as "no dependents"
Reflects the index as of the last index run; the freshness envelope and the per-dependent `stale` flags state how far that is from the files on disk
tools.performance: Warm, five-run measurements on the three declared tiers, with the exact commands and raw runs in validation/tools/bb_impact/LATENCY.json. All three tiers are inside budget on the current index. Fixture tiers: p50 83.8 ms / p95 100.8 ms on test/fixtures/polyglot/ts-js and p50 176.5 ms / p95 243.5 ms on the 100-file synthetic scale fixture, both default-argument calls. Reference large index (.bb-data, 11,440 files, ~3.4 GB, measured through the tool's byte-read-only open with the index's own files hashed before and after, `dbUnchanged: true`): per-symbol p95 was 327.7 ms for the widest studied hub (`join`), 321.2 ms for `named`, 236.0 ms for `refReachable` and 153.6 ms for `computeImpact` — every measured call stayed inside the 5 s budget, and p50s were 42.9–284.2 ms. The walk's per-symbol caller query is planned through `brain_symbol_project_owner_idx` for the owner range and `brain_rel_proj_type_target_idx` for the relationship filter, so the cost is index-bounded. One correction belongs on the record: an earlier campaign measurement on THIS index returned 13.7–359.5 s for default calls, and a hand-built comparison attributed it to the engine's owner-cascade JOIN form (10,351 ms against 12.5 ms for a flat target-indexed form). That measurement predates the owner-range index and the planner state now on disk; re-measured byte-read-only on the current index, the same JOIN form answers in 1.1 ms and the walk in 40–63 ms. The absolute millisecond figures belong to the machine, so the fixture-tier numbers are the regression baselines this tool holds.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data. Staleness repair, when it runs, reindexes changed files through the shared bounded auto-refresh budget and never rewrites source.
tools.evidence: Impact derives from brain_relationship rows through the same graph engine the editor impact panel uses. The returned set is the engine's caller traversal under the declared dependency kinds, owner cascade, noise policy and depth; the declared total is an INDEPENDENT bounded walk under exactly that rule, so it is the size of the set the answer is a prefix of. Completeness is PROVED rather than inferred: whenever truncation was declared or the walk reached the last expandable depth, the set is measured against an unbounded walk of the same rule, so an answer that is short of the whole truth says so even when no bound fired (measured: cobra `HasAvailableFlags` answers 28 with `truncated: true` instead of 27 with `truncated: false`), and an engine row cap that hides no dependent no longer masquerades as a truncation. Evidence lives in validation/tools/bb_impact/ (AUDIT.md, LATENCY.json, probes, latency-t2-query-cost.json) and in the gate evidence of the three verifiers named below.

tools.name: bb_cross_language
tools.description: Cross-language facts for one symbol from stored brain_relationship rows only (is_cross_language = 1), per-pair with bridge mechanism and evidence tier. Every fact names both ends — the copy of the requested name it came from and the other symbol's name, file, language and line — plus the stored row id. A name is many symbols (the index holds one per file/name/line), so facts are the union over every copy; `copies` names them and `ambiguous` says so. SEPARATELY, `memberFacts` holds the rows on the copies' MEMBERS: each fact's `self` is the MEMBER the stored row names, `owner` is the copy of the asked name it was attributed through, and `pair` is exactly `self.language → other.language` (null when the two are equal or unknown, and then the row is counted in `unpairableRowCount` rather than given a pair). Member rows are the MEMBER's edges, never absorbed into the symbol's — `ownFactCount`, `memberFactCount` and `silentItselfButNotItsMembers` tell the two apart. Absence is a property of the store: it is declared only when neither the copies nor their direct members hold a stored row. A row that exists but cannot name a language pair is NOT absence — it is counted in `unpairableRowCount` and named in `pairlessRowNote`, while `storedRowCount` still reports it. Rows on descendants at depth 2 or deeper are counted in `deeperDescendantRowCount` (both directions) and deliberately not cascaded. Counts name what they count: `factCount` facts in this answer, `pairCount` DISTINCT language pairs, `signatureCount` distinct (pair, direction, bridge, tier); `memberCount` is the distinct members that contributed BEFORE the limit while `memberFactCount` is what was shown, and `ownFactsTruncated`/`memberFactsTruncated` say which section a limit cut. The answer is bounded by `limit` (default 200, max 1000) with `truncated` and `totalCountIfKnown` declared, and the copy list has its own declared cap. This tool never infers, guesses, or aspires. Same source and laws as the editor's cross-language hover section.

symbol.description: symbol name to fetch cross-language facts for (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

limit.description: max facts to return (default 200, max 1000); truncation is declared, never silent. Refused below 1 or above 1000 rather than clamped

documentation.summary: Stored cross-language pairs, each naming both ends, with member rows reported separately as the member's, absence declared as a property of the store, and declared bounds and truncation.

returns: One fact per stored cross-language row about the name. `facts` holds the rows on the copies themselves; `memberFacts` holds the rows on their MEMBERS. Every fact names both ends — `self` (symbol, file, language, line) and `other` — plus the stored `rowId`, direction, bridge, evidence tier and confidence. **The fact-shape invariant:** `self` is the endpoint the STORED ROW NAMES (the copy for `match: "exact"`, the member for `match: "owner-cascade"`), so `pair` is always exactly `self.language → other.language` and any consumer can re-derive it. A member fact also carries `owner` — the copy of the asked name it was attributed through — and `matchedMember`/`matchedMemberId`, which are the member end and its stored id (a mirror of `self`, kept so either name reads the same)

`copies`: every indexed symbol carrying the name, with file, language, line and cross-row count, plus `ambiguous` and `ambiguityNote`. `limit` governs FACTS; the copy list has its own cap — `copiesCap`, with `copiesTruncated` and a `copiesNote` when it bites. `copyCount` is always the TRUE total from its own query, never the length of a capped array, so `ambiguous` cannot be silenced by the cap

Counts name what they count: `factCount` is the number of facts in this answer; `pairCount` is the number of DISTINCT language pairs in it (`"java → kotlin"` is one pair however many rows carry it); `signatureCount` is the number of distinct (pair, direction, bridge, tier) signatures; `totalCountIfKnown` is the number of facts that exist before the limit. `ownFactCount` and `memberFactCount` are the facts shown per section, and `ownFactsTruncated` / `memberFactsTruncated` say which section the budget cut. `memberCount` is the distinct members that contributed a member fact BEFORE the limit, so it can exceed `memberFactCount`

Declared absence is a property of the STORE, not of the emitted facts: `declaredAbsent` is true only when neither the copies nor their direct members hold a stored cross-language row, and `absenceNote` says so — scoped to the project, because that is what the row queries searched. A row that exists but cannot name a language pair is NOT absence: it is counted in `unpairableRowCount`, the empty fact set is explained in `pairlessRowNote`, and `storedRowCount` still reports it

`deeperDescendantRowCount` counts stored cross-language rows on descendants at depth 2 or deeper, BOTH directions, and does not cascade them into the facts (a descendant's edges are the descendant's). When the owner itself is silent but such rows exist, the absence note names the count instead of claiming the index holds nothing

Declared truncation: `truncated`, `truncationReason` and `totalCountIfKnown` when the `limit` bounded the facts. `collapsedRowCount` counts a row matched from both directions and emitted once; a row that is counted there is never emitted twice
errors: Missing or blank symbol (refused, not defaulted)
Symbol not found in the index — a declared error, not an empty set
limit outside the declared 1..1000 range, a fractional limit, or a non-number limit — refused, never clamped silently
limitations: THE MEMBER CASCADE IS ONE LEVEL DEEP. A member's rows are reported as the member's, with the owner named; a grandchild's rows are counted in `deeperDescendantRowCount` and deliberately not emitted as the owner's or the member's. Ask about the descendant directly to see them

Stored rows only. Nothing here infers an edge, a bridge mechanism or a tier. Every fact traces to a `brain_relationship` row with `is_cross_language = 1`, filtered by the ROW's own project id in this tool and in the editor's cross-language hover section, so a row minted for another project cannot appear as a fact about this one

The absence note is scoped to ONE PROJECT: the same name indexed in another project may hold rows for it, and `absenceNote` says which store it searched rather than claiming anything about the whole index

`bridge` is stored data, not an inference about communication. On indexed corpora almost every row carries the indexer's name-resolution placeholder, so a bridge value names how the row was minted, not a verified interop mechanism. A row with no stored mechanism renders a fixed `unnamed bridge` text rather than an invented one

A name held by many symbols is answered as the UNION over all of them; every fact names the copy it came from, so an agent can narrow, but the tool never chooses one copy on the agent's behalf and does not resolve which copy a human means

Rows that cannot name a pair are counted, not dropped: an endpoint whose file has no detected language, or two endpoint languages that are equal, produces no fact and increments `unpairableRowCount`. No shipped corpus reaches that state today, so it is verified by seeding the state rather than assumed — and a row that exists but cannot name a pair is reported as `pairlessRowNote`, never as absence
`memberCount` describes the whole answer, while `memberFactCount` describes what the limit showed. When the two differ, `memberFactsTruncated` is true and `truncationReason` names the budget

Tier classification is a stored-vs-derived contract: when the indexer stored `metadata.evidenceClass` the stored class is rendered; otherwise the derived rule in `src/lsp/evidence_tier.ts` is used. `confidence` is the stored row confidence and is rendered beside the tier, never instead of it
tools.performance: Measured with `validation/tools/bb_cross_language/work/latency.mts` (warm, five runs, p50/p95, machine load recorded) and `work/latency-t2-handler.mts` on a COPY of the 6,452-file reference index (6452 files, 310,423 symbols, 820,040 relationships). Tiny fixture (5 files, 5 stored cross-language rows): p50 8.3 ms / p95 8.6 ms. Synthetic 97-file single-language repository (the absence path): p50 38.9 ms / p95 59.7 ms. Reference index, handler against the copy, default arguments: `Command` p50 7.6 ms / p95 7.8 ms; `file` (3,457 copies) p50 112 ms / p95 169 ms; `type` (5,392 copies) p50 278 ms / p95 328 ms — 15x inside the 5 s ceiling. The two by-name statements and the depth>=2 count are index-driven on purpose: written naively they scanned the project's 820,040 relationship rows (measured 3.8–17.6 s per statement, p50 3.3–6.5 s per call, one sample at 33.6 s). Forcing the walking order to start at the symbol-name index and at the recursive descendant table — with every predicate preserved, proved row-set identical on a 692-file corpus with 714 stored rows — took one name from 14,641 ms to 26 ms and the depth count from 1.4–1.7 s to 5–36 ms. Both the pre-fix and post-fix rounds stay in `LATENCY.json` as the regression baseline.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data.
tools.evidence: Only `brain_relationship` rows with `is_cross_language = 1`, filtered by the ROW's own project id — in both this tool and the editor cross-language hover section — and by nothing else: no graph walk, no lexical id-prefix cascade, no inferred pair. Every fact carries the stored row id and both ends, so a reader can re-check it against the store without trusting the tool. Tiers are delegated to the single classifier in `src/lsp/evidence_tier.ts` over the declared derivation, so the same stored row cannot render two different tiers on two surfaces. Member rows follow the store's `owner_symbol_id` ownership edge, while `bb_graph`'s cascade is a lexical id-prefix range, so the two counts differ by design; the answer states which rule it used rather than reconciling the numbers. Cross-checked on a 692-file, 8-language corpus with 714 stored cross-language rows (403 checks, 16 planted defects all caught), against seeded store states no corpus reaches (43 seeded checks, 8 planted defects including a ROW-LEVEL project-predicate leak, each caught by a probe proved false on the unmutated code), and against the editor's hover projection (21 checks, 5 planted defects; both surfaces read the same owner module). See validation/m63/results/CL1.json, validation/tools/bb_cross_language/results/GATE.json and validation/m26/results/W3.json.

tools.name: bb_annotate
tools.description: Attach an agent-authored annotation to a symbol in the shared index. Provenance is enforced: `author_class` is hardcoded 'agent' for tool writes (a tool call cannot write a 'human' note), and the row records the caller's self-declared `toolIdentity` plus timestamps. Re-annotating the same symbol+path updates the note in place and reports the note it replaced — one note per author per location is enforced by a unique index over (project, symbol, author, path). The symbol is not checked against the index; the reply MEASURES whether an editor surface can show the note and says so in `surfacing`. `editor` is the JOINT truth the hover and graph badge use: the name (or qualified name) must be indexed AND declared in the resolved file, so a name indexed only in another file is reported `editor: false` with the reason rather than promised. `path` resolves to the index's own spelling, so `src/a.ts`, `./src/a.ts` and the absolute path are the same note. Declared bounds: body 2000 chars, toolIdentity 200 chars, symbol 500 chars, path 1024 chars — refusals, never truncation. Annotations are opinions layered on evidence, never index facts. On a project with no index, the first write creates that project's annotation store and `surfacing.editor` is false. To change source code use bb_edit; to read notes back use bb_annotations.

symbol.description: symbol name to annotate, max 500 chars (`target`/`query` are accepted as aliases); it is not required to exist in the index — reachability is measured and reported

body.description: annotation text, max 2000 chars counted in code points (an astral glyph is one character); empty or whitespace-only is refused
